item.title: Multinational Enterprises and the Sustainable Development Goals: Evolving Roles, Challenges, and Opportunities Beyond 2030
item.content:encoded:
Huda Khan, University of Aberdeen

Hussain Rammal, Adelaide University

Pervez Ghauri, University of Birmingham

Zaheer Khan, University of Aberdeen

Martin Meyer, University of Vaasa

The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), adopted in 2015, provide a comprehensive global agenda addressing critical social, economic, and environmental challenges, with the target of achieving these goals by 2030. These 17 interconnected goals range from eradicating poverty and ensuring quality education to combating climate change and fostering sustainable economic growth. As the global community works toward this ambitious target, the role of Multinational Enterprises (MNEs) has become increasingly vital. MNEs, with their significant financial resources, innovation capabilities, and extensive global reach, are uniquely positioned to contribute meaningfully to the realization of these global objectives. However, integrating the SDGs into business strategies presents considerable challenges, especially in light of evolving institutional, political, and social dynamics.

In this context, it is essential to critically assess the progress made by MNEs in supporting the SDGs, focusing not only on successes but also on areas where progress has stalled or where the current trajectory requires recalibration. As the world struggles to meet the deadline for the SDG agenda, there is an urgent need to reassess the contributions of MNEs and to explore how these enterprises can adapt in response to the shifting global landscape. This will ensure that MNEs' operations remain aligned with the sustainability and social equity goals. Additionally, the rise of backlash against Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) initiatives presents new challenges that may influence MNEs' strategies, especially their long-term commitment to the SDGs as we move beyond 2030.

This special issue aims to explore the evolving and multifaceted role of MNEs in advancing the SDGs, with a dual focus on the remaining years of the current SDG agenda and the post-2030 sustainability framework. We aim to assess how MNEs can contribute meaningfully to achieving the SDGs by 2030 while addressing the complexities of changing political, social, and economic contexts. Furthermore, how these enterprises will adapt to, and engage in shaping, sustainability frameworks beyond 2030, particularly given the shifting global trends and the growing scepticism surrounding ESG commitments.

MNEs are critical enablers of global sustainability due to their market power, innovation potential, and financial resources. With their global value chains spanning several nations, MNEs influence the markets in which they operate and impact the communities. As key players in industrial transformation, they can drive positive change by aligning their business strategies with the SDGs. Their ability to innovate, scale sustainable practices, and set industry standards enables them to be significant actors in addressing global challenges, such as climate change, poverty, and inequality. They can drive disruptive societal change through their global experience.

However, MNEs' involvement in the SDGs must extend beyond mere profit-driven motives. To contribute effectively to the SDGs, MNEs must prioritize inclusive business practices and environmental stewardship, ensuring that their operations create shared value across economic, social, and environmental dimensions. This involves addressing global inequalities through inclusive business models, promoting responsible production and consumption, and investing in sustainable innovations that mitigate long-term global risks, such as resource depletion, biodiversity loss, and climate change.

Integrating the SDGs into business operations is a complex and multifaceted endeavour. MNEs face several barriers, including institutional inertia, political uncertainties, and varying regulatory frameworks across different markets. The political economy of each host country significantly influences how effectively SDGs can be pursued, particularly in regions with weak governance systems or where sustainability initiatives are not adequately incentivized. Moreover, cross-sector collaboration models that are often considered essential for addressing complex SDG challenges can be hindered by competing interests or regulatory barriers.

Internally, MNEs face challenges aligning sustainability strategies with shareholder interests. The increasing pressure to deliver short-term financial performance can sometimes conflict with the long-term investments required for sustainable development. Measuring the impact of MNE activities on the SDGs also presents a significant challenge, with accountability and transparency emerging as critical issues. While frameworks for impact measurement and reporting are still evolving, many MNEs struggle to quantify their contributions to the SDGs in ways that are meaningful to stakeholders.

As we approach the final years of the SDG agenda, it is important to critically reflect on the lessons learned thus far and evaluate where gaps remain. While many MNEs have made significant strides toward integrating the SDGs into their operations, the pace of change has been uneven across industries and regions. For instance, in sectors such as renewable energy, MNEs have made substantial contributions toward achieving SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy). In contrast, other areas, such as climate action (SDG 13) and responsible consumption (SDG 12), still face significant challenges.

Looking beyond 2030, the post-SDG sustainability framework will necessitate that MNEs adapt to an increasingly complex landscape. Political shifts, economic transformations, and societal changes are likely to continue shaping the global sustainability agenda. Evolving ESG expectations, alongside the increasing backlash against these initiatives, will play a pivotal role in shaping how businesses engage with the SDGs. As societal expectations around climate action, diversity, and corporate responsibility grow, MNEs will need to navigate a delicate balance between business imperatives and public expectations.

This dynamic context requires MNEs to adopt a long-term perspective, committing to sustainable business practices that focus not only on short-term financial returns but also on their broader impact on global sustainability. The post-2030 agenda may require MNEs to take on more active roles in developing global frameworks for climate action, economic inclusivity, and social equity, with greater accountability and transparency in reporting their contributions toward these goals.

The evolving role of MNEs in shaping global sustainability frameworks necessitates an integrated approach to International Business (IB) and Business and Society (BAS) scholarship. By merging insights from the IB and societal domains, a more comprehensive understanding of the factors that drive MNEs' engagement with the SDGs can be developed, alongside the mechanisms through which they can exert influence. Understanding the interplay between these factors is crucial for both academia and practitioners, who seek to guide MNEs toward more effective sustainability practices that drive tangible, long-term impacts.

By examining both the successes and shortcomings of MNEs in relation to the SDGs, this special issue aims to explore strategies for scaling successful initiatives, overcoming barriers, and adapting to a rapidly changing global environment. The goal is to provide actionable insights that can guide MNEs in navigating the complex terrain of SDGs' integration and contribute to the development of a post-2030 sustainability framework that is inclusive, equitable, and resilient in the face of future challenges.

Potential topics

  • MNEs' Evolving Role in the SDGs' Agenda: Achievements, Gaps, and Future Directions - How can MNEs evaluate their contributions to the SDGs and adjust their strategies to meet the 2030 targets? What opportunities and challenges will MNEs face post-2030 in continuing to support the SDGs' agenda? How can MNEs address the lagging targets of the SDGs in their operations?
  • Managing ESG Backlash and its impact on MNEs' SDGs' Alignment - How does the ESG backlash impact MNEs' strategies for achieving the SDGs? In what ways do political and institutional pressures shape MNEs' SDG agendas? How can MNEs maintain their commitment to the SDGs amidst the growing scepticism toward ESG?
  • Institutional Dynamics and MNEs' SDGs' Engagement - How do formal and informal institutional logics influence MNEs' strategies for addressing SDGs in different host countries? How do institutional voids in emerging markets shape MNEs' SDG engagement? What roles do institutional actors (governments, NGOs, civil society) play in shaping MNEs' SDG commitments?
  • Business and Society Perspectives on MNEs and SDGs: Bridging IB and B&S Literature - How can IB literature inform B&S's understandings of MNEs' contributions to SDGs? How do MNEs reconcile profit motives with societal goals in their SDGs' strategies? What are the synergies between business model innovation and sustainable development in the context of the SDGs?
  • Leveraging Global Value Chains for Sustainable Development - What practical strategies can MNEs adopt to integrate sustainability into their global value chains to meet SDGs' targets? What are the opportunities for MNEs to collaborate with supply chain partners on SDGs' initiatives? How can knowledge transfer across value chains improve SDGs' outcomes?
  • Organizational Forms and Alliance for SDGs: Bridging IB and BAS Perspectives - How can MNEs and their partners in cross-sector alliances navigate the challenges of aligning values, beliefs, and power dynamics in SDG-driven initiatives? In what ways can partnerships between MNEs, governments, NGOs, and CSOs enhance the achievement of SDGs, particularly in areas such as inclusive development and climate action? What role do MNE headquarters play in supporting subsidiaries and local network partners to integrate global sustainability principles into their operations? How can MNEs collaborate with SMEs to achieve SDGs, and what benefits does this collaboration bring to local communities? How do strategic alliances contribute to the long-term sustainability of SDG initiatives, and what organizational forms are most effective in fostering these collaborations?
  • Micro-foundations of MNEs' Engagement with SDGs: Motivations, Leadership, and Human Capital - How do the personal experiences and values of top management, including the CEO, influence MNEs' strategies for addressing the SDGs? What role does diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) play in shaping top management's engagement with sustainability goals and advancing SDGs? How do leadership styles and top management teams influence employee engagement with SDG initiatives within MNEs? What mechanisms within MNEs' governance structures support or hinder the integration of SDGs into business models, particularly in the areas of poverty eradication, climate action, and social equity? How do individual decision-makers contribute to business model innovations that advance SDGs, and how do these innovations affect the company's long-term sustainability efforts?

item.title: OR for Sustainability in Supply Chain Management
item.content:encoded:
Kannan Govindan, University of Southern Denmark

Organizations must rethink and optimize their existing strategies to meet their sustainable business goals, due to the constant depletion of vital resources and the greater demands of societal issues. The increasing population not only has an impact on natural resources, but it also results in greater pollution and contributes to greater levels of poverty. With these considerations, on September 25, 2015, some countries adopted a new set of sustainability development goals (SDGs) to end poverty and to improve prosperity worldwide. Seventeen sustainable development goals have been targeted to achieve by 2030 under the new sustainable development agenda. Further, these sustainable development goals encompass a range of perspectives and various levels of applications, including supply chain management. In recent years, researchers and practitioners have addressed supply chain management issues because of their significant impacts on organizational developments regardless of the field of applications. Over the years, researchers have proven that an inefficient supply chain can force an organization to fail. Hence, integrating SDGs in operations and supply chain management areas is an important topic to explore. Many studies sought to explore sustainability in supply chain management with a wide range of concepts and strategies, including green, lean, and other approaches with a special focus on newly targeted SDGs. Research is needed to further analyze and shape the implementation of SDGs in supply chain management environments with the help of advanced operations research (OR) methods, including multi-attribute decision making (MADM) and multi-objective decision making (MODM).

The main objective of this special section is to invite academic practitioners to contribute a better understanding of the scientific basis for decoupling economic growth from resource depletion and environmental degradation while improving human lives with the assistance of advanced OR methods. It is believed that advanced optimization models and algorithms can improve data-driven decision models by either formulating pattern discoveries and knowledge extraction problems or by defining efficient algorithms for implementing SDGs in supply chain management at a macro level. Additionally, new algorithms continually make efficiency gains and improve the applicability of older algorithms. Virtually every numerical analysis includes several optimization algorithms that can be applied to design sustainability in supply chain. With these concerns, this special section pertains to sustainable supply chain management (SSCM) by making direct connections between resources, the environment, the economy, and the goal of achieving SDGs in different parts of the world through OR methods.

These themes should incorporate an integrated approach: looking at possibilities of connecting the conservation of resources with sustainable human economic activities (from a supply chain perspective), and monitoring progress towards sustainable indicator strategies with the support of multi stakeholders in predominant inter- and intra- organizational management fields. This special section will comprise a significant body of knowledge about how natural resources are being utilized in various economies and will address the impact of this use on the eco-efficient and socio-economic systems, and suggest pathways of transitioning to a more sustainable future. This perspective includes building on and expounding the significance of resource conservation and efficiency along with a societal focus to improve sustainable development in supply chain management by achieving the proposed SDGs.

This special section seeks to be specific regarding the different kinds of sustainable supply chains because they can affect the policy implications of different sustainable indicators. In addition to these ideas, this special section welcomes authors to contact us to discuss other possible subtopics. To encourage effective methods and thereby motivate the authors to adopt a variety of sustainable supply chain perspectives in approaching this subject, the special section Editor has purposely kept the above list of suggested topics short. However, all submissions must suit within the domain statement of the journal.

Potential topics

  • Designing and policymaking in SDGs through stakeholder support: to provide examples of sustainable policy and design making with multi-stakeholder perspectives and to define how sustainability is considered in framing policies and enumerating success factors and challenges on supply chain management
  • Implementing SDGs in supply chains through innovative strategies and practices: to identify the sustainable goals, indicators, and practices related to the implementation of sustainable supply chain management and to explore how this knowledge may be used to effectively manage and conserve resources with less environmental and societal impact
  • Monitoring supply chain governance and implications with a focus on SDGs: to elaborate practices and supporting mechanisms in measuring, monitoring, and reporting progress toward achieving targets, and to further emphasize various challenges related to the implementation of SDGs in supply chain management in different applications/context/economies

item.title: A Decade (2015-2025) of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): Trends, Reflections, and Realignments in Hospitality and Tourism Research
item.content:encoded:
Edmund Goh, Les Roches Abu Dhabi Hospitality Academy

Jun Wen, Macau University of Science and Technology

Siamak Seyfi, University of Oulu

C. Michael Hall, Massey University

Xin-Jean Lim, Sun Yat-Sen University

September 2025 marked the 10th anniversary of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), a global blueprint for achieving peace, prosperity, and planetary wellbeing. Over the past decade, the hospitality and tourism industries and destination communities have emerged as powerful platforms for advancing and contesting these goals. Hospitality and tourism encompass all 17 SDGs, either directly or indirectly, from economic growth and decent work (SDG 8) to responsible consumption and production (SDG 12), climate action (SDG 13), and partnerships for the goals (SDG 17).

In hospitality and tourism research, SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) has guided studies on workforce inclusion, ethical employment, and skills development; SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) has inspired frameworks for food-waste reduction, sustainable procurement, and circular-economy innovation; and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) has informed investigations into heritage protection, destination resilience, and overtourism management. At the same time, SDG 5 (Gender Equality) and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) have underpinned studies on women's empowerment, migrant labour, and social inclusion across tourism enterprises. Research has also expanded around SDG 13 (Climate Action) and SDG 14/15 (Life Below Water and Life on Land), addressing carbon measurement, biodiversity conservation, and regenerative destination practices.

While studies have advocated that tourism and hospitality can positively contribute to the fulfilment of the UN's ambitious 2030 Agenda, there remains a noticeable gap in how the SDGs are explicitly integrated within scholarly research. Many studies have investigated sustainability-related themes without explicitly aligning their objectives, frameworks, or findings to specific SDG targets, often downplaying or omitting the SDG lens altogether. This disconnect limits the sector's ability to evaluate progress, benchmark impact, and influence policymaking.

This Special Issue responds to those calls by encouraging tourism and hospitality researchers to explicitly reconnect their work to the SDG framework, to identify future research pathways, and to assist policymakers in addressing global challenges through evidence-based strategies. In particular, we seek contributions that illuminate the dynamic linkages between key stakeholders such as hosts, tourists, destinations, government, and industry to explore how these interrelationships can generate more sustainable and equitable outcomes.

This Special Issue seeks to critically assess the progress, limitations, and future directions of SDG-related initiatives in hospitality and tourism. We invite empirical, conceptual, and review papers that evaluate how far the sector has come but also envision pathways for a regenerative, inclusive, and just hospitality and tourism future beyond 2030.

Potential topics

  • Reflecting on the First Decade (2015–2025) of SDG achievements and gaps
  • Critical reviews of how research to date references SDGs and where conceptual or methodological gaps persist
  • Evaluating tourism and hospitality's contribution to all 17 SDGs, including SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) through community tourism, local sourcing, and food redistribution
  • Examining progress toward SDG 3 (Good Health and Wellbeing) through wellness tourism, workplace health initiatives, and traveller safety
  • Assessing SDG 4 (Quality Education) via tourism and hospitality curriculum transformation, sustainability literacy, and lifelong learning
  • Policy coherence and alignment of tourism strategies with SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions), focusing on governance, transparency, and ethical practices
  • Reviewing the role of SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure) in sustainable destination design, transport systems, and smart tourism
  • Integrating SDG 8 (Decent Work), SDG 5 (Gender Equality), and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) through inclusive recruitment, fair wages, and leadership opportunities
  • Advancing SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) via food waste management, circular hospitality systems, and sustainable event management
  • Strengthening SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) by aligning urban tourism, heritage conservation, and destination capacity management
  • Building SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals) through cross-sector collaborations among government, academia, and private enterprises
  • Linking SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) and SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) to energy-efficient hotel design, water conservation, and waste-water reuse
  • Exploring SDG 13 (Climate Action), SDG 14 (Life Below Water), and SDG 15 (Life on Land) through carbon-neutral travel, biodiversity protection, and eco-restoration tourism
  • Applying SDG 9 (Innovation and Infrastructure) and SDG 16 (Institutions) in AI-driven sustainability measurement, blockchain transparency, and smart destination governance
  • Embedding SDG 3 (Health) and SDG 11 (Communities) in wellness, resilience, and crisis recovery frameworks
  • Integrating ethical, cultural, and spiritual perspectives on sustainability to support SDG 4 (Education) and SDG 17 (Partnerships)
  • Conceptualising post-SDG paradigms such as regenerative tourism, circular hospitality, etc.
  • Examining the intersections of sustainability with digital transformation, big data, and tourism intelligence systems
  • Developing cross-SDG frameworks and metrics to capture interlinkages (e.g., SDG 8–12–13 synergies)
  • Big data analytics, AI, and social media mining for SDG progress tracking and destination reporting
  • Comparative cross-national or longitudinal studies assessing tourism's SDG impact
  • Theorising host–guest–destination dynamics as a holistic system contributing to SDG 1–17 interdependence
